claim: Intestinal nematodes such as human hookworms infect almost 500 million people worldwide.
source: Intestinal nematodes such as human hookworms are highly successful parasites, infecting almost 500 million people worldwide (Loukas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loukas et al., 2016.

claim: Intestinal nematodes are associated with immunosuppression.
source: They are associated with immunosuppression (Bethony et al., 2006), which in turn may reduce the prevalence of immune-mediated diseases such as asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bethony et al., 2006.

claim: Hookworm-infected populations tend to have a lower prevalence of diseases such as allergy and asthma.
source: Epidemiological studies indicate that hookworm-infected populations tend to have a lower prevalence of diseases such as allergy and asthma (Leonardi-Bee et al., 2006), although analysis of these studies is complicated by readouts of allergic disease, timing, dose and species of parasitic infection, and non-infectious socioeconomic factors (McSorley et al., 2019; Santiago and Nutman, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leonardi-Bee et al., 2006, McSorley et al., 2019, and Santiago and Nutman, 2016.

claim: Suppression of allergic pathology is seen after parasitic infection in animal models.
source: Studies in animal models of parasitic infection support this association, with suppression of allergic pathology seen after parasitic infection (Chenery et al., 2016; Obieglo et al., 2018; Smits et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chenery et al., 2016; Obieglo et al., 2018; Smits et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2005.

claim: Parasite secretions have immunosuppressive capacity in mouse models of asthma.
source: Suppression of allergic responsiveness or tolerization of the host to parasite and bystander allergens has been hypothesised to be through the release of immunomodulatory secretions from the parasite, which has been supported by numerous studies in mouse models of asthma showing the immunosuppressive capacity of parasite secretions (Buck et al., 2014; Ebner et al., 2014; Finlay et al., 2017; McSorley et al., 2014; McSorley et al., 2012; Trujillo-Vargas et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buck et al., 2014; Ebner et al., 2014; Finlay et al., 2017; McSorley et al., 2014; McSorley et al., 2012; Trujillo-Vargas et al., 2007.

claim: The IL-33 pathway has critical importance in type two immune responses in allergy.
source: The IL-33 pathway has critical importance in type two immune responses both in allergy (Bønnelykke et al., 2014) and helminth parasite ejection (Coakley et al., 2017; Hung et al., 2013), thus it could be a central factor in parasite immunomodulation and the prevention of asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bønnelykke et al., 2014.

claim: The IL-33 pathway has critical importance in helminth parasite ejection.
source: The IL-33 pathway has critical importance in type two immune responses both in allergy (Bønnelykke et al., 2014) and helminth parasite ejection (Coakley et al., 2017; Hung et al., 2013), thus it could be a central factor in parasite immunomodulation and the prevention of asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coakley et al., 2017; Hung et al., 2013.

claim: IL-33 is an alarmin cytokine released from epithelial, endothelial and stromal cells on necrotic cell death.
source: IL-33 is an alarmin cytokine, released from epithelial, endothelial and stromal cells on necrotic cell death caused by noxious stimuli, such as allergen or pollutant inhalation, infections and mechanical damage (Johansson and McSorley, 2019; Mahlakõiv et al., 2019; Spallanzani et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johansson and McSorley, 2019; Mahlakõiv et al., 2019; Spallanzani et al., 2019.

claim: Mast cells can be an important source of IL-33 in H. polygyrus infection.
source: Recent studies also show that mast cells can also be an important source of IL-33 in H. polygyus infection, secreting the cytokine in response to damage signals from epithelial cells (Shimokawa et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shimokawa et al., 2017.

claim: Extracellular IL-33 binds to its receptor complex consisting of ST2 and IL-1RAcP.
source: Extracellular IL-33 binds to its receptor complex, consisting of ST2 (Il1rl1) and the IL-1 Receptor Accessory Protein (IL1RAcP) (Günther et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Günther et al., 2017.

claim: IL-33 receptor signalling induces IL-5 and IL-13 production by type two innate lymphoid cells.
source: IL-33 receptor signalling induces IL-5 and IL-13 production by type two innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s), IL-6 from mast cells and IFNγ from NK and γδT cells (Cayrol and Girard, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cayrol and Girard, 2018.

claim: IL-33 receptor signalling induces IL-6 from mast cells.
source: IL-33 receptor signalling induces IL-5 and IL-13 production by type two innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s), IL-6 from mast cells and IFNγ from NK and γδT cells (Cayrol and Girard, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cayrol and Girard, 2018.

claim: IL-33 receptor signalling induces IFNγ from NK and γδT cells.
source: IL-33 receptor signalling induces IL-5 and IL-13 production by type two innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s), IL-6 from mast cells and IFNγ from NK and γδT cells (Cayrol and Girard, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cayrol and Girard, 2018.

claim: HpARI binds to DNA and IL-33 in necrotic host cells, tethering the cytokine in the nucleus.
source: From studies of the murine model intestinal nematode Heligmosomoides polygyrus, we recently identified the H. polygyrus Alarmin Release Inhibitor (HpARI), a protein secreted by a murine intestinal nematode which binds to DNA and IL-33 in necrotic host cells, tethering the cytokine in the nucleus, preventing its release while simultaneously directly blocking binding to its receptor ST2 (Osbourn et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Osbourn et al., 2017.

claim: HpARI directly blocks IL-33 binding to its receptor ST2.
source: From studies of the murine model intestinal nematode Heligmosomoides polygyrus, we recently identified the H. polygyrus Alarmin Release Inhibitor (HpARI), a protein secreted by a murine intestinal nematode which binds to DNA and IL-33 in necrotic host cells, tethering the cytokine in the nucleus, preventing its release while simultaneously directly blocking binding to its receptor ST2 (Osbourn et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Osbourn et al., 2017.

claim: Hp-TGM is a mimic of host TGF-β which induces regulatory T cells.
source: H. polygyrus also secretes Hp-TGM, a mimic of host TGF-β which induces regulatory T cells (Johnston et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnston et al., 2017.

claim: Both HpARI and Hp-TGM consist of a string of consecutive atypical Complement Control Protein domains.
source: Intriguingly, both HpARI and Hp-TGM consist of a string of consecutive atypical Complement Control Protein domains (CCP/Sushi/SCR domains, Interpro IPR000436).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Interpro IPR000436.

claim: Proteins containing CCP domains are greatly expanded in H. polygyrus.
source: As proteins containing CCP domains are greatly expanded in H. polygyrus (Maizels et al., 2018), and many of these CCP domain-containing proteins are secreted (Hewitson et al., 2013) we hypothesised that the CCP domain-containing family represents an immunomodulatory family of proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maizels et al., 2018.

claim: Many CCP domain-containing proteins in H. polygyrus are secreted.
source: As proteins containing CCP domains are greatly expanded in H. polygyrus (Maizels et al., 2018), and many of these CCP domain-containing proteins are secreted (Hewitson et al., 2013) we hypothesised that the CCP domain-containing family represents an immunomodulatory family of proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hewitson et al., 2013.

claim: HpBARI consists of two atypical CCP domains.
source: Here, we identify the H. polygyrus Binds Alarmin Receptor and Inhibits (HpBARI), a protein secreted by the parasite which consists of two atypical CCP domains.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI inhibits cell surface detection of ST2.
source: HpBARI binds murine ST2, inhibiting cell surface detection of ST2, preventing IL-33-ST2 interactions, and inhibiting IL-33 responses in vitro and in an in vivo mouse model of asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI prevents IL-33-ST2 interactions.
source: HpBARI binds murine ST2, inhibiting cell surface detection of ST2, preventing IL-33-ST2 interactions, and inhibiting IL-33 responses in vitro and in an in vivo mouse model of asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI inhibits IL-33 responses in vitro.
source: HpBARI binds murine ST2, inhibiting cell surface detection of ST2, preventing IL-33-ST2 interactions, and inhibiting IL-33 responses in vitro and in an in vivo mouse model of asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI inhibits IL-33 responses in an in vivo mouse model of asthma.
source: HpBARI binds murine ST2, inhibiting cell surface detection of ST2, preventing IL-33-ST2 interactions, and inhibiting IL-33 responses in vitro and in an in vivo mouse model of asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ST2 detection is abrogated in the peritoneal cavity during H. polygyrus infection.
source: In H. polygyrus infection, ST2 detection is abrogated in the peritoneal cavity and lung, consistent with systemic effects of HpBARI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ST2 detection is abrogated in the lung during H. polygyrus infection.
source: In H. polygyrus infection, ST2 detection is abrogated in the peritoneal cavity and lung, consistent with systemic effects of HpBARI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 binds human ST2 with high affinity.
source: HpBARI_Hom2 also binds human ST2 with high affinity, and effectively blocks human PBMC responses to IL-33.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 effectively blocks human PBMC responses to IL-33.
source: HpBARI_Hom2 also binds human ST2 with high affinity, and effectively blocks human PBMC responses to IL-33.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: H. polygyrus blocks the IL-33 pathway via HpARI which blocks the cytokine.
source: Thus, we show that H. polygyrus blocks the IL-33 pathway via both HpARI which blocks the cytokine, and also HpBARI which blocks the receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations in the manuscript.

claim: H. polygyrus blocks the IL-33 pathway via HpBARI which blocks the receptor.
source: Thus, we show that H. polygyrus blocks the IL-33 pathway via both HpARI which blocks the cytokine, and also HpBARI which blocks the receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both HES and HpARI can suppress eosinophilia and ILC2 responses.
source: While both HES and HpARI could suppress eosinophilia and ILC2 responses (McSorley et al., 2014; Osbourn et al., 2017), we found significant differences in ST2 detection on lung ILC2s.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McSorley et al., 2014; Osbourn et al., 2017.

claim: HpARI reduced levels of ST2 to that of the PBS control.
source: Alternaria allergen administration induced increased expression of ST2, and while HpARI reduced levels of ST2 to that of the PBS control (presumably due to blockade of IL-33 signalling) we found that HES suppressed detection of ST2 on ILC2s to levels far below baseline (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: HES suppressed detection of ST2 on ILC2s to levels far below baseline.
source: Alternaria allergen administration induced increased expression of ST2, and while HpARI reduced levels of ST2 to that of the PBS control (presumably due to blockade of IL-33 signalling) we found that HES suppressed detection of ST2 on ILC2s to levels far below baseline (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Detection of ST2 on lung ILC2s was reduced in a dose-dependent fashion when HES was added.
source: Detection of ST2 on lung ILC2s was reduced in a dose-dependent fashion when HES was added (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 and Hp_I25217_IG17161_L558 are closely-related genes encoding CCP domain-containing proteins with 87% identity.
source: Of the 20 candidate proteins which proteomic analysis indicated most accurately correlated with the ST2-suppressive effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), two were closely-related genes encoding CCP domain-containing proteins (Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 and Hp_I25217_IG17161_L558, 87% identity).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Purified recombinant Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 showed a dose-dependent ability to suppress ST2 detection on lung ILC2s in vitro.
source: Purified recombinant Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 showed a dose-dependent ability to suppress ST2 detection on lung ILC2s in vitro, acting at ~100 fold lower concentration than total HES (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 acts at ~100 fold lower concentration than total HES.
source: Purified recombinant Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 showed a dose-dependent ability to suppress ST2 detection on lung ILC2s in vitro, acting at ~100 fold lower concentration than total HES (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 dose-dependently suppressed IL-5, IL-6 and IL-13 production by bone marrow cells cultured with IL-2, IL-7 and IL-33.
source: Culture of naïve murine bone marrow cells with a combination of IL-2, IL-7 and IL-33 induced production of IL-5, IL-6 and IL-13, all of which were dose-dependently suppressed by the Hp_I25642_IG17586_L548 protein (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: HpBARI consists of two CCP domains, each containing four conserved cysteines and a tryptophan between the third and fourth cysteine residue.
source: The HpBARI protein consists of two CCP domains, each containing four conserved cysteines and a tryptophan between the third and fourth cysteine residue (Kirkitadze and Barlow, 2001; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and citation to Kirkitadze and Barlow, 2001.

claim: A stretch of genomic DNA in the published H. polygyrus genome shows 97% identity to the HpBARI sequence over five exons.
source: A Wormbase ParaSite BLAST search for HpBARI in the published H. polygyrus genome was carried out (Howe et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2017), identifying a stretch of genomic DNA showing 97% identity to the HpBARI sequence over five exons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST search data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and citations to Howe et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2017.

claim: Each CCP domain in HpBARI is encoded over two exons, with intron/exon boundaries falling between each CCP domain.
source: As expected for a CCP domain protein, each CCP domain was encoded over two exons, with intron/exon boundaries falling between each CCP domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Johnston et al., 2017; Osbourn et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and citations to Johnston et al., 2017; Osbourn et al., 2017.

claim: The C-terminal region of the HpBARI protein is critical for its binding and function.
source: The C-terminal region of the HpBARI protein appears to be critical for its binding and function, as when HpBARI was expressed with C-terminal purification tags (HpBARI_C), its activity was ablated in in vitro IL-33 suppression assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recombinant HpBARI suppressed Alternaria-induced BAL and lung eosinophilia 24 hr after allergen administration.
source: When recombinant HpBARI was co-administered with Alternaria allergen, it suppressed Alternaria-induced BAL and lung eosinophilia, ILC2 activation and soluble type 2 cytokines 24 hr after allergen administration (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), at a timepoint where responses are independent of the adaptive immune response (Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011.

claim: Recombinant HpBARI suppressed ILC2 activation 24 hr after Alternaria allergen administration.
source: When recombinant HpBARI was co-administered with Alternaria allergen, it suppressed Alternaria-induced BAL and lung eosinophilia, ILC2 activation and soluble type 2 cytokines 24 hr after allergen administration (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), at a timepoint where responses are independent of the adaptive immune response (Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011.

claim: Recombinant HpBARI suppressed soluble type 2 cytokines 24 hr after Alternaria allergen administration.
source: When recombinant HpBARI was co-administered with Alternaria allergen, it suppressed Alternaria-induced BAL and lung eosinophilia, ILC2 activation and soluble type 2 cytokines 24 hr after allergen administration (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), at a timepoint where responses are independent of the adaptive immune response (Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011.

claim: Responses 24 hr after Alternaria allergen administration are independent of the adaptive immune response.
source: When recombinant HpBARI was co-administered with Alternaria allergen, it suppressed Alternaria-induced BAL and lung eosinophilia, ILC2 activation and soluble type 2 cytokines 24 hr after allergen administration (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), at a timepoint where responses are independent of the adaptive immune response (Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bartemes et al., 2012; Kouzaki et al., 2011.

claim: H. polygyrus Acetylcholinesterase (HpAChE) is a control protein secreted by H. polygyrus adult worms.
source: This activity was specific to the HpBARI protein, as suppressive effects could not be replicated by administration of H. polygyrus Acetylcholinesterase (HpAChE) - a control protein secreted by H. polygyrus adult worms (Accession No. JF439067) (Hewitson et al., 2011), expressed in the same system as HpBARI (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hewitson et al., 2011 and experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: HpBARI administered at day 0 was able to suppress BAL and lung eosinophilia in an Alternaria-OVA model of asthma.
source: Furthermore, we utilized an Alternaria-OVA model of asthma in which Alternaria allergen is used to induce a Th2 immune response against OVA protein in the lungs, which can be recalled by later administration of OVA protein alone (Osbourn et al., 2017). HpBARI administered at day 0 was able to suppress BAL and lung eosinophilia, and ILC2 and CD4+ T cell IL-13 production, although in the case of ILC2 IL-13 production this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D and citation to Osbourn et al., 2017.

claim: HpBARI administered at day 0 was able to suppress ILC2 and CD4+ T cell IL-13 production in an Alternaria-OVA model of asthma.
source: Furthermore, we utilized an Alternaria-OVA model of asthma in which Alternaria allergen is used to induce a Th2 immune response against OVA protein in the lungs, which can be recalled by later administration of OVA protein alone (Osbourn et al., 2017). HpBARI administered at day 0 was able to suppress BAL and lung eosinophilia, and ILC2 and CD4+ T cell IL-13 production, although in the case of ILC2 IL-13 production this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D and citation to Osbourn et al., 2017.

claim: HpBARI administration resulted in significant abrogation of the ST2 signal to far below baseline levels on total CD45+ lung cells.
source: HpBARI administration, alone or co-administered with Alternaria allergen, resulted in significant abrogation of the ST2 signal to far below baseline levels in the PBS group, on total CD45+ lung cells (Figure 5A) or gated ILC2s (Figure 5B), similarly to that with HES administration (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 1A-B.

claim: HpBARI administration resulted in significant abrogation of the ST2 signal to far below baseline levels on gated ILC2s.
source: HpBARI administration, alone or co-administered with Alternaria allergen, resulted in significant abrogation of the ST2 signal to far below baseline levels in the PBS group, on total CD45+ lung cells (Figure 5A) or gated ILC2s (Figure 5B), similarly to that with HES administration (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 1A-B.

claim: HpBARI did not suppress ST2 transcription below baseline levels.
source: However, when ST2 transcription was assessed by qPCR, no suppression below baseline levels of ST2 transcription was seen with HpBARI administration (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HpBARI suppressed eosinophilia 24 hr after Alternaria allergen administration, even when a single dose of HpBARI was given 24 hr prior to allergen.
source: We found that HpBARI suppressed eosinophilia 24 hr after Alternaria allergen administration, even when a single dose of HpBARI was given 24 hr prior to allergen (Figure 5D), while lung ILC2 ST2 suppression by HpBARI had similar kinetics (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Lung ILC2 ST2 suppression by HpBARI had similar kinetics to eosinophilia suppression.
source: We found that HpBARI suppressed eosinophilia 24 hr after Alternaria allergen administration, even when a single dose of HpBARI was given 24 hr prior to allergen (Figure 5D), while lung ILC2 ST2 suppression by HpBARI had similar kinetics (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HpBARI could be detected on the surface of lung ILC2s up to 7 days after administration.
source: Using avidin-PE staining of biotinylated HpBARI, we found that HpBARI could be detected on the surface of lung ILC2s (but not control ST2-negative lung cells) up to 7 days after administration, although this signal only reached statistical significance when HpBARI was co-administered with Alternaria allergen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HpBARI was not detected on control ST2-negative lung cells.
source: Using avidin-PE staining of biotinylated HpBARI, we found that HpBARI could be detected on the surface of lung ILC2s (but not control ST2-negative lung cells) up to 7 days after administration, although this signal only reached statistical significance when HpBARI was co-administered with Alternaria allergen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strong suppression of ST2 staining was found in the peritoneal lavage ILC2 populations during H. polygyrus infection.
source: Although little to no detectable ST2 staining was found on ILC2s of the mesenteric lymph node (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D) (consistent with recent findings [Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2019]), strong suppression of ST2 staining was found in the peritoneal lavage and lung ILC2 populations (Figure 6A–D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C, and citations to Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2019.

claim: Strong suppression of ST2 staining was found in the lung ILC2 populations during H. polygyrus infection.
source: Although little to no detectable ST2 staining was found on ILC2s of the mesenteric lymph node (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D) (consistent with recent findings [Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2019]), strong suppression of ST2 staining was found in the peritoneal lavage and lung ILC2 populations (Figure 6A–D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C, and citations to Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2019.

claim: Little to no detectable ST2 staining was found on ILC2s of the mesenteric lymph node during H. polygyrus infection.
source: Although little to no detectable ST2 staining was found on ILC2s of the mesenteric lymph node (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D) (consistent with recent findings [Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2019]), strong suppression of ST2 staining was found in the peritoneal lavage and lung ILC2 populations (Figure 6A–D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-D and citations to Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2019.

claim: A highly granular lineage-negative population in the peritoneal lavage expressed very high levels of ST2 in naïve mice.
source: Strikingly, a highly granular lineage-negative population in the peritoneal lavage (most likely mast cells [Enoksson et al., 2013]) expressed very high levels of ST2 in naïve mice, which was strongly suppressed during H. polygyrus infection (Figure 6E–F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, and citation to Enoksson et al., 2013.

claim: ST2 expression on a highly granular lineage-negative population in the peritoneal lavage was strongly suppressed during H. polygyrus infection.
source: Strikingly, a highly granular lineage-negative population in the peritoneal lavage (most likely mast cells [Enoksson et al., 2013]) expressed very high levels of ST2 in naïve mice, which was strongly suppressed during H. polygyrus infection (Figure 6E–F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, and citation to Enoksson et al., 2013.

claim: HpBARI bound mouse ST2-Fc in a dose-dependent manner in a solid-phase ELISA assay.
source: HpBARI bound mouse ST2 or IL-33-TRAP in a dose-dependent manner, while control plates coated with HpARI (expressed in the same system with the same tags) did not show any binding to these constructs (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: HpBARI bound mouse IL-33-TRAP in a dose-dependent manner in a solid-phase ELISA assay.
source: HpBARI bound mouse ST2 or IL-33-TRAP in a dose-dependent manner, while control plates coated with HpARI (expressed in the same system with the same tags) did not show any binding to these constructs (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: HpARI did not show any binding to mouse ST2-Fc or IL-33-TRAP in a solid-phase ELISA assay.
source: HpBARI bound mouse ST2 or IL-33-TRAP in a dose-dependent manner, while control plates coated with HpARI (expressed in the same system with the same tags) did not show any binding to these constructs (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: HpBARI was depleted from solution and immunoprecipitated by ST2-Fc.
source: These data were confirmed using an immunoprecipitation approach, conjugating ST2-Fc and IL-33-TRAP to protein G beads. Confirming the ELISA data, HpBARI was depleted from solution and immunoprecipitated by ST2 or IL-33-TRAP (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HpBARI was depleted from solution and immunoprecipitated by IL-33-TRAP.
source: These data were confirmed using an immunoprecipitation approach, conjugating ST2-Fc and IL-33-TRAP to protein G beads. Confirming the ELISA data, HpBARI was depleted from solution and immunoprecipitated by ST2 or IL-33-TRAP (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Biotinylated HpBARI bound strongly to wild-type ILC2s.
source: To confirm the specificity of HpBARI binding to ST2, biotinylated HpBARI was incubated for 20 min at 4°C with bone marrow-derived ILC2s from either wild-type or ST2-deficient mice. HpBARI bound strongly to wild-type ILC2s, while no binding of biotinylated HpARI to wild-type ILC2s, or biotinylated HpBARI to ST2-deficient ILC2s could be seen (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No binding of biotinylated HpARI to wild-type ILC2s could be seen.
source: To confirm the specificity of HpBARI binding to ST2, biotinylated HpBARI was incubated for 20 min at 4°C with bone marrow-derived ILC2s from either wild-type or ST2-deficient mice. HpBARI bound strongly to wild-type ILC2s, while no binding of biotinylated HpARI to wild-type ILC2s, or biotinylated HpBARI to ST2-deficient ILC2s could be seen (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No binding of biotinylated HpBARI to ST2-deficient ILC2s could be seen.
source: To confirm the specificity of HpBARI binding to ST2, biotinylated HpBARI was incubated for 20 min at 4°C with bone marrow-derived ILC2s from either wild-type or ST2-deficient mice. HpBARI bound strongly to wild-type ILC2s, while no binding of biotinylated HpARI to wild-type ILC2s, or biotinylated HpBARI to ST2-deficient ILC2s could be seen (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Pre-incubation of ILC2s with HES ablated binding of biotinylated HpBARI.
source: Pre-incubation of ILC2s with either HES or unlabeled HpBARI ablated binding of biotinylated HpBARI, while maintaining suppression of ST2 (Figure 7D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), further supporting the specificity of this interaction, and showing that HpBARI in HES was responsible for the suppression of ST2 detection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pre-incubation of ILC2s with unlabeled HpBARI ablated binding of biotinylated HpBARI.
source: Pre-incubation of ILC2s with either HES or unlabeled HpBARI ablated binding of biotinylated HpBARI, while maintaining suppression of ST2 (Figure 7D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), further supporting the specificity of this interaction, and showing that HpBARI in HES was responsible for the suppression of ST2 detection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HpBARI in HES was responsible for the suppression of ST2 detection.
source: Pre-incubation of ILC2s with either HES or unlabeled HpBARI ablated binding of biotinylated HpBARI, while maintaining suppression of ST2 (Figure 7D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), further supporting the specificity of this interaction, and showing that HpBARI in HES was responsible for the suppression of ST2 detection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HpBARI ablated ST2 detection with both RM-ST2-2 and DIH9 antibodies.
source: In order to assess whether HpBARI suppression was specific to the antibody used for ST2 detection, we compared ST2 detection by clone RM-ST2-2 (ThermoFisher) to clone DIH9 (Biolegend), but found that HpBARI ablated ST2 detection with both antibodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HpBARI showed high affinity for mouse ST2 with a Kd of 0.26 nM.
source: HpBARI showed high affinity for mouse ST2 (k+=4 μM−1s−1, k–=1.1×10−3 s−1, Kd = 0.26 nM) and IL-33-TRAP (k+=3.9 μM−1s−1, k–=6.5×10−4 s−1, Kd = 0.17 nM) (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: HpBARI showed high affinity for mouse IL-33-TRAP with a Kd of 0.17 nM.
source: HpBARI showed high affinity for mouse ST2 (k+=4 μM−1s−1, k–=1.1×10−3 s−1, Kd = 0.26 nM) and IL-33-TRAP (k+=3.9 μM−1s−1, k–=6.5×10−4 s−1, Kd = 0.17 nM) (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: C-terminal-tagged HpBARI had an off-rate ~4 fold faster than the N-terminal tagged construct.
source: When C-terminal-tagged HpBARI was tested in the SPR assay, although it could still bind to IL-33-TRAP the construct's off-rate was found to be ~4 fold faster than the N-terminal tagged construct (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), giving some explanation for its abrogated function (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: HpBARI prevented the interaction of IL-33 with its receptor.
source: To assess whether the binding of HpBARI to the IL-33 receptor inhibited IL-33 ligation, protein G microbeads were coated with ST2-Fc or IL-33-TRAP, and HpBARI was allowed to bind. IL-33 was then added to the beads and precipitation of IL-33 assessed by western blot, showing that HpBARI could prevent the interaction of IL-33 with its receptor (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Heat-treatment of HpBARI partially abrogated its ability to prevent IL-33-receptor interaction.
source: This interaction was partially abrogated by heat-treatment of HpBARI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI ablated IL-33 binding to IL-33-TRAP in surface plasmon resonance assays.
source: The inhibition of IL-33-ST2 interaction by HpBARI was confirmed by surface plasmon resonance: mouse IL-33-TRAP was used to coat a protein G chip, HpBARI was bound, and IL-33 binding assessed. IL-33 gave a robust response on binding to IL-33-TRAP, which was ablated on preincubation of HpBARI (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: HpBARI showed far lower binding to human ST2 than to mouse ST2.
source: HpBARI was tested for binding to human ST2 and found to show far lower binding to the human than to the mouse form of the IL-33 receptor (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: HPOL_0001228401 encodes a protein with 58% identity to HpBARI.
source: However, homology searching via Wormbase Parasite (Howe et al., 2017) identified the H. polygyrus gene HPOL_0001228401 encoding a protein with 58% identity to HpBARI which we named HpBARI_Hom2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by homology search data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and citation to Howe et al., 2017.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 can be detected on a western blot probed with anti-HpBARI polyclonal rat IgG.
source: HpBARI_Hom2 has a similar enough structure to HpBARI that it can be detected on a western blot probed with anti-HpBARI polyclonal rat IgG, which also detects a faint band in HES, indicating the presence of these proteins in endogenous H. polygyrus secretions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Anti-HpBARI polyclonal rat IgG detects a faint band in HES, indicating the presence of HpBARI-like proteins in endogenous H. polygyrus secretions.
source: HpBARI_Hom2 has a similar enough structure to HpBARI that it can be detected on a western blot probed with anti-HpBARI polyclonal rat IgG, which also detects a faint band in HES, indicating the presence of these proteins in endogenous H. polygyrus secretions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 showed far greater binding to human ST2 than HpBARI.
source: When this protein was expressed, it was found to show far greater binding to human ST2 (Figure 8A) than HpBARI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 bound more strongly to human ST2 (Kd = 0.062 nM) than to mouse ST2 (Kd = 0.138 nM).
source: SPR experiments confirmed that HpBARI_Hom2 bound more strongly to human ST2 (k+=4.8 μM−1s−1, k–=2.98×10−4 s−1, Kd = 0.062 nM) than to mouse ST2 (k+=7.18 μM−1s−1, k–=9.56×10−4 s−1, Kd = 0.138 nM) (Figure 8B–C; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 8B-C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 blocked interaction of human IL-33 with human ST2.
source: As with HpBARI and mouse ST2, HpBARI_Hom2 blocked interaction of human IL-33 with human ST2. In a SPR assay, the signal seen when human IL-33 was allowed to bind to a human ST2-coated chip was ablated when HpBARI_Hom2 was injected first (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 showed a significantly increased ability to block human IL-33-ST2 interaction compared to HpBARI in an ELISA assay.
source: Furthermore, when an oxidation-resistant form of human IL-33 (Cohen et al., 2015) was coated onto an ELISA plate and probed with human ST2, HpBARI_Hom2 showed a significantly increased ability to block human IL-33-ST2 interaction compared to HpBARI (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8D and citation to Cohen et al., 2015.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 blocked IL-33-induced IFN-γ production from human PBMCs with an average IC50 of 16 nM.
source: HpBARI_Hom2 blocked IL-33-induced IFN-γ production from human PBMCs (average IC50 of 16 nM or 480 ng/ml, measured by ELISA), while HpBARI had far lower activity (IC50 of >1000 nM (Figure 8E)).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: HpBARI had far lower activity in blocking IL-33-induced IFN-γ production from human PBMCs (IC50 of >1000 nM).
source: HpBARI_Hom2 blocked IL-33-induced IFN-γ production from human PBMCs (average IC50 of 16 nM or 480 ng/ml, measured by ELISA), while HpBARI had far lower activity (IC50 of >1000 nM (Figure 8E)).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 is a high-affinity binder of human ST2.
source: Therefore, HpBARI_Hom2 is a high-affinity binder of human ST2, and a functional suppressor of human IL-33 responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI_Hom2 is a functional suppressor of human IL-33 responses.
source: Therefore, HpBARI_Hom2 is a high-affinity binder of human ST2, and a functional suppressor of human IL-33 responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: H. polygyrus releases miRNA-containing extracellular vesicles which downregulate the transcription of ST2.
source: H. polygyrus also releases miRNA-containing extracellular vesicles which downregulate the transcription of ST2 (Buck et al., 2014) and an unknown factor which induces IL-1β release, counter-regulating IL-33 responses (Zaiss et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buck et al., 2014.

claim: H. polygyrus releases an unknown factor which induces IL-1β release, counter-regulating IL-33 responses.
source: H. polygyrus also releases miRNA-containing extracellular vesicles which downregulate the transcription of ST2 (Buck et al., 2014) and an unknown factor which induces IL-1β release, counter-regulating IL-33 responses (Zaiss et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zaiss et al., 2013.

claim: ST2 is expressed at a far lower level on ILC2s in the intestine compared to those from the lung, fat or bone marrow.
source: Recent papers have noted that ST2 is expressed at a far lower level on ILC2s in the intestine compared to those from the lung, fat or bone marrow (Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2018.

claim: Extracellular vesicles secreted by H. polygyrus reduce pulmonary ST2 expression when delivered directly to the lung.
source: Interestingly, extracellular vesicles secreted by H. polygyrus have also been shown to reduce pulmonary ST2 expression when delivered directly to the lung (Buck et al., 2014), but our data are the first to suggest systemic reduction in ST2 detection during intestinal helminth infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buck et al., 2014.

claim: This study provides the first evidence to suggest systemic reduction in ST2 detection during intestinal helminth infection.
source: Interestingly, extracellular vesicles secreted by H. polygyrus have also been shown to reduce pulmonary ST2 expression when delivered directly to the lung (Buck et al., 2014), but our data are the first to suggest systemic reduction in ST2 detection during intestinal helminth infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpBARI can bind effectively to both membrane-bound and soluble forms of ST2.
source: Our ELISA, immunoprecipitation, SPR and flow cytometry data show that HpBARI can bind effectively to both membrane-bound and soluble forms of ST2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Full-length IL-33 is presumed to have a lower affinity for ST2 than processed forms.
source: On release, IL-33 is processed by endogenous and exogenous proteases from the full-length protein, stored in the nucleus, to a series of smaller processed forms with increased activity (Cayrol et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2018). Full-length IL-33 is presumed to have a lower affinity for ST2 than processed forms, however these measurements have not to date been directly made.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cayrol et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2018 and speculation.

claim: HpBARI can outcompete the highest-affinity mature form of IL-33 for binding to ST2.
source: HpBARI can outcompete the highest-affinity mature form of IL-33 for binding to ST2, therefore we conclude that HpBARI could abrogate signals from all forms of IL-33.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference in the manuscript.

claim: ST2 is constitutively expressed on the surface of many cell types.
source: The advantage of targeting ST2 rather than IL-33 is that ST2 is constitutively expressed on the surface of many cell types, and therefore could be blocked prior to damage and IL-33 release.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: IL-33 is constitutively expressed in the nucleus of epithelial cells.
source: IL-33, while constitutively expressed in the nucleus of epithelial cells, is released transiently on damage, and has a very short-lived active form (Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2015.

claim: IL-33 has a very short-lived active form.
source: IL-33, while constitutively expressed in the nucleus of epithelial cells, is released transiently on damage, and has a very short-lived active form (Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2015.

claim: The H. polygyrus genome contains >80 CCP domain-containing proteins.
source: The H. polygyrus genome contains >80 CCP domain-containing proteins (Maizels et al., 2018), many of which can be detected in the parasite's secretions (Hewitson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maizels et al., 2018.

claim: An IL-13-binding protein from the intestinal parasite Trichuris muris was recently identified.
source: Recently, an IL-13-binding protein from the intestinal parasite Trichuris muris was identified (Bancroft et al., 2019), indicating that direct binding interactions with molecules of the host immune system are not unique to H. polygyrus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bancroft et al., 2019.

claim: Strains of H. polygyrus infect wood mice, groove-toothed harvest mice, reed voles, and Mus musculus.
source: Strains of H. polygyrus infect wood mice (Apodemus sylvaticus), groove-toothed harvest mice (Reithrodontomys spp.) and reed voles (Microtus spp) as well as Mus musculus (Forrester, 1971; Kim et al., 2015), host species which have a common ancestor 15–20 million years ago (Steppan and Schenk, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forrester, 1971; Kim et al., 2015.

claim: Host species infected by H. polygyrus have a common ancestor 15–20 million years ago.
source: Strains of H. polygyrus infect wood mice (Apodemus sylvaticus), groove-toothed harvest mice (Reithrodontomys spp.) and reed voles (Microtus spp) as well as Mus musculus (Forrester, 1971; Kim et al., 2015), host species which have a common ancestor 15–20 million years ago (Steppan and Schenk, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Steppan and Schenk, 2017.

claim: H. polygyrus may have developed subfamilies of its immunomodulators selected for peak efficacy in each host species.
source: Thus H. polygyrus may have developed subfamilies of its immunomodulators, which have been selected for peak efficacy in each host species.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the data presented.
